content: The recommendations outlined in the guideline will also be published as a commentary in a peer-reviewed journal, adhering to the World Health Organization's (WHO) open-access and copyright policies. The WHO Department of Reproductive Health and Research, in collaboration with non-governmental organizations and professional associations, will assist national and subnational working groups in adapting and implementing the guideline. This process will involve the development or revision of existing national guidelines or protocols to align with the new recommendations. The GREAT Network (Guideline-driven, Research priorities, Evidence synthesis, Application of evidence, and Transfer of knowledge) strategy can be employed to convene relevant stakeholders. This approach will help identify priorities, barriers, and facilitators for guideline implementation and support stakeholders in creating implementation strategies tailored to their local contexts. Technical support will be provided to local implementers for the development of training manuals, flow charts, and quality indicators, as well as participation in stakeholder meetings. The WHO recommendations on non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections will be disseminated widely. An Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) for maternal and perinatal health recommendations convenes annually to review WHO’s current portfolio of recommendations, prioritize new and existing questions, and determine the need for updates. The recommendations in this guideline will undergo regular review and prioritization by the Executive GSG as necessary. The WHO Steering Group will continue to monitor research developments related to cesarean sections, particularly in areas where evidence is lacking or of low certainty. New recommendations or changes to existing ones may be warranted based on emerging evidence. Decisions to update the guideline will also be informed by data from ongoing studies identified through trial registry searches. Following the publication and dissemination of the guideline, any concerns regarding the validity of a recommendation will be promptly communicated to implementers and will inform plans for updates. All technical products developed during the guideline development process, including systematic review reports, search strategies, Cochrane RevMan files, and GRADE quality ratings, have been archived for future reference. If new evidence raises concerns about the validity of a recommendation, the relevant systematic review will be updated. Any new questions identified during a scoping exercise at the end of five years will undergo a similar process of evidence retrieval, synthesis, and grading in accordance with WHO standards for guideline development. In collaboration with the Steering Group, WHO will periodically assess the currency of the recommendations and the need for new or updated guidance. This will involve scoping exercises with technical experts, healthcare professionals, researchers, and service users to identify controversial or priority areas requiring evidence-based guidance. The WHO Departments of Reproductive Health and Research, and Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health welcome suggestions for additional questions to be included in future updates of the guideline.
